name: Prison Policy Initiative (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: incarcerated people and their families in the United States (federal phone caps, state free-call laws, decarceration).
summary: Prison Policy Initiative is a small US research and advocacy group on mass incarceration (1.9 million dollars spent in the year to June 2025). Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average over the wins of those years: a share of the federal caps on prison and jail phone rates that the Martha Wright-Reed Act of 2022 made possible (still saving families about 250 million dollars a year after the FCC raised the caps in 2025), a smaller share of five states' free-call laws and other fee and visiting wins, a very small share of the people kept out of prison by the reforms its data fed (their better years and the deaths a year in prison causes), and half the credit for ending prison gerrymandering in several states, each valued on the site's shared scales; every branch is discounted for missing data. The result is about 0.06 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, a little below the median of the site's global-health models: half of it is deaths averted by decarceration, while money saved by poor American families is worth little on a scale set by the world's poorest, and PPI holds about five years of spending in reserve, so the next dollar counts at a quarter of the average. The biggest uncertainties are PPI's share of the decarceration and phone-rate campaigns and how long the caps hold.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: PPI's spending (one programme column), averaged over fiscal years 2021-2025 (the years the wins below come from) in 2025 prices, with its share of management and fundraising. From the audited statements and Forms 990.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: What the wins of the period cover: families' yearly savings from the federal caps and the state free-call laws, and the people the reforms keep out of prison or jail.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What each dollar saved and each year out of prison is worth on the site's scales, and the years each win counts, discounted.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Consumption per person in families of incarcerated people (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: People in prison and their families are mostly poor: the shared US survey consumption per person times the poorest fifth's spending share, which is per household, turned into per person with the shared household sizes (the poorest fifth's households are smaller), as the site's other US models do.

rows.label: Federal caps: phone-company owners' consumption as a multiple of the national average
rows.explainer: The part of the savings that comes out of the phone companies' margins falls on their owners, mostly private-equity funds and their investors, who are well off: 2 times the national-accounts average, from 1 to 4.

rows.label: Federal caps: share of the savings that comes out of commissions to prisons and jails
rows.explainer: Before the caps, providers paid prisons and jails commissions out of call revenue, which the 2024 order banned from the rates; that part of the families' savings is lost by county and state budgets, the rest by the providers. Commissions often ran at half or more of jail call revenue; our judgment 40% of the savings, from 20% to 60%.

rows.label: Federal caps: value of a dollar families save, net of what the payers lose (units of value)
rows.explainer: On the site's log scale a small change in consumption is worth the dollars over consumption per person (spread over a household, household size cancels): the families' gain less the payers' loss, the payers at the national-accounts mean (the site's rule for everyone's consumption): lost commissions as state and local money (the shared payer multiple and cost of public funds), the providers' share at their owners' multiple.

rows.label: State laws: value of a dollar families save, net of the taxpayers' cost (units of value)
rows.explainer: As above, with the state taxpayers' dollar raised at the shared cost of public funds and the shared state and local payer multiple.

rows.label: Yearly savings to families the FCC's 2024 caps would have brought

source.title: Worth Rises, FCC votes unanimously to significantly lower phone and video communication costs (18 July 2024)
source.quote: the new rules will save impacted families at least $500 million annually

rows.explainer: The FCC's July 2024 order under the Martha Wright-Reed Act (2022), which for the first time covered calls within a state: advocates put the savings at at least $500 million a year, the FCC's draft at $386 million. Our estimate 450 million, from 386 to 550 million.

rows.label: Share of the 2024 caps' savings lost when the FCC raised the caps in October 2025

source.title: Worth Rises, Worth Rises condemns FCC rollback of correctional telecom regulations (29 October 2025)
source.quote: will deliver substantially less financial relief to families impacted by incarceration — at least $215 million less per year

rows.explainer: The interim caps of October 2025 (11 cents a minute at most prisons, 10 to 19 cents at jails, in effect from 5 December 2025 and to be met by 6 April 2026, Prison Legal News) are higher than the 2024 caps but still cap in-state jail calls that had cost up to 11.35 dollars for 15 minutes at some large jails (ABA Journal, July 2024). Worth Rises puts the relief lost at at least 215 million of its at least 500 million (43%); the share is taken from that one frame and applied to our total: 43%, from 40% to 60% ("at least" leaves more room above).

rows.label: Share of the federal savings already counted under the state free-call laws
rows.explainer: Where calls are free (California, Minnesota and Colorado prisons, Massachusetts and Connecticut prisons and jails) the caps save nothing more. Those prisons already charged less than the new caps, so the overlap is in Massachusetts' and Connecticut's jails, a small part of the country's jail calls: 2%, from 0 to 5%.

rows.label: Interstate calls' share of the savings the 2024 caps would have brought
rows.explainer: Most calls from prisons and jails are to people in the same state, which is why the 2022 Act's extension of the FCC's power to in-state calls mattered; our judgment 15% of the 2024 savings, from 5% to 30%.

rows.label: The 2021 interstate cut as a share of the 2024 cut on the same calls
rows.explainer: From 21 cents to 12 at prisons in 2021 (9 cents) against 21 to 6 cents in 2024 (15 cents) is 0.6; at jails 21 to 14 (7 cents) against 21 to 6-9 cents (12-15 cents) about 0.5; many providers already charged less than the old cap, so less was cut in practice: 45%, from 25% to 70%.

rows.label: Yearly savings from the FCC's 2021 cut of interstate caps
rows.explainer: In May 2021 the FCC cut interstate caps from 21 cents a minute to 12 cents at prisons and 14 at large jails (Third Report and Order, Federal Register 28 July 2021). Its savings are the 2024 order's, scaled by the interstate share of calls and by the 2021 cut against the 2024 one. Counted only until the later caps covered the same calls, within the shared years a win counts; credited, valued and adjusted as the later federal caps are.

rows.label: Yearly savings to families under the caps in force
rows.explainer: What the federal win still saves families each year: mostly in jails, since 94% of prisons already charge less than the new caps (Prison Legal News), less the overlap with the state laws. The FCC's 2021 interstate cut is added in its own row.

rows.label: Years from the federal win until it takes effect
rows.explainer: The Act passed in January 2023; caps that bind took effect in December 2025 and must be met by April 2026: about 3 years, from 2 to 4.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: People held by Connecticut's Department of Correction (prisons and jails), October 2023

source.title: Connecticut Office of Policy and Management, Monthly Indicators Report, October 2023

rows.explainer: Connecticut runs one system for prisons and jails, all covered by the free-call law of 2021 (at least 90 minutes a person a day).

rows.label: Connecticut: yearly saving per person held
rows.explainer: Worth Rises' 2026 report finds free calls save 172 to 1,801 dollars per incarcerated person a year across the systems that made them free (Truthout); Connecticut's calls were among the most expensive in the country before the law, so it sits in the upper part: 1,200 dollars, from 500 to the report's top of 1,801.

rows.label: Connecticut: yearly savings from free prison calls (law of 2021)
rows.explainer: Connecticut's people held times the yearly saving per person; no published total.

rows.label: Colorado: yearly savings from free prison calls (law of 2023)
rows.explainer: Free calls in state prisons, phased in until July 2025; no published total. About 17,000 people in prison at 172 to 600 dollars each a year (the low end and the lower part of the range in Worth Rises' 2026 report, Truthout): 6 million, from 2 to 10 million.

rows.label: Yearly savings from the state free-call laws of 2021-2023
rows.explainer: The five state laws passed in the period; New York's (July 2025) came after it and isn't counted. The state branch also carries the other state and local money wins (fee_savings_per_year).

rows.label: Yearly savings from ending medical copays and capping release-card and commissary fees in the period
rows.explainer: A few state prison systems ended medical copays in the period while others kept pandemic waivers: tens of thousands of people at copays of 2 to 5 dollars a visit, a few visits a year, under a million dollars; plus caps on release-card and commissary fees, on which PPI published the national data. No total is published: our judgment 2 million, from 0.5 to 8 million.

rows.label: Yearly savings from bans on replacing in-person visits with paid video calls
rows.explainer: State and county rules of the period that keep in-person visits where jails had moved to paid video calls (a practice PPI put on the national radar in 2015). Jail video calls cost families several dollars for 20 minutes; a few states and counties acted, so tens of thousands of people held at a few visits a month: our judgment 2 million, from 0.5 to 8 million.

rows.label: Yearly savings from the other state and local money wins
rows.explainer: Credited, valued and adjusted as the state free-call laws are: the same families, the same public payers, the same coalitions.

rows.label: Years from the state laws until free calls began
rows.explainer: California's and Massachusetts' free calls began months after the laws passed, Colorado's were phased in over two years: 0.5, from 0 to 1.5.

rows.label: State laws: discounted years of impact
State laws and other money wins: value per campaign year, before adjustments (units of value)
Fewer people incarcerated through the reforms of 2020-2025 PPI's research and support fed
rows.explainer: PPI supplies the data behind bail, sentencing, parole and jail-expansion fights and gave technical support to advocates in 24 states (audit note 1). The country held nearly 2 million people in 2025, about 13% below the pre-pandemic level (The Whole Pie 2025), much of the fall from the pandemic itself and some refilled since. Local fights against jail expansion count here too. Our judgment: the reforms won in the period keep 50,000 people out, from 10,000 to 150,000.

rows.label: Wellbeing gained per person-year out of prison or jail (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for what a year of incarceration costs in life satisfaction (facts/incarceration.json). Read only by the decarceration branch; the phone branches are valued in money.

rows.label: Years from the reforms until fewer people are held
rows.explainer: Bail and parole changes act within months, sentencing changes over years: 0.5, from 0 to 2.

rows.label: Decarceration: discounted years of impact
Decarceration: WELLBYs per campaign year, before adjustments
Years of life lost per year in prison or jail
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/incarceration.json): about 2 years of life per year served (Patterson 2013), read by every model that counts years of incarceration averted. Deaths, not wellbeing: the life-satisfaction figure above is the quality of the years a person does live.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison or jail
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/incarceration.json): turns years of life lost into a share of a death.

rows.label: Years from a prison-year averted until the deaths it would have caused
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/incarceration.json).

rows.label: Value of a death averted at prison ages
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death at ages 15-49 (most people in prison or jail), times the shared multiplier.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person-year kept out of prison or jail
rows.explainer: Years of life lost per year held, as a share of a death at the remaining life expectancy.

rows.label: Discount for the delay until the deaths
rows.explainer: The wait until the deaths a prison-year would have caused, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Decarceration: deaths averted, units of value per campaign year, before adjustments
rows.formula: dec_people * dec_deaths_per_person_year * dec_value_per_death * dec_discounted_years * dec_death_delay_discount / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Same people, years and wait as the wellbeing term (dec_value_per_year), valued as deaths averted. It adds to the life-satisfaction term and does not repeat it: that counts how much better each year outside is than a year inside, for years the person lives; this counts the years of life a prison-year takes away afterwards (mostly after release), which carry no wellbeing in the other term.

rows.label: People in the communities whose representation the end of prison gerrymandering restored
rows.explainer: Counting incarcerated people at their home address for redistricting, a change PPI's campaign has won in more than a dozen states, several of them for the 2021 redistricting in this period. It moves representation back to the (mostly poor, mostly urban) neighbourhoods people in prison come from; our judgment of the people in districts whose weight changed noticeably: 2 million, from 0.5 to 5 million.

rows.label: Wellbeing gained per person a year from fairer representation (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: No study measures it. Reference class: Frey and Stutzer (2000, Economic Journal) find residents of the Swiss canton with the most direct-democracy rights about 11 percentage points more likely to be completely satisfied with life than those of the canton with the fewest; with most people moving up one or two points on the 0-10 scale, that is roughly 0.1 to 0.2 points on the mean, part of it procedural (the satisfaction of having a say). Ending prison gerrymandering changes a district's weight by a few percent of its population, so scaling that difference by the share of voice restored gives at most about 0.004; these residents already vote, so the procedural part doesn't move: our judgment 0.0003 points a year, from 0 to 0.004.

rows.label: Years from the change until districts are redrawn
rows.explainer: The changes apply at the next redistricting: those of the period took effect with the 2021-2022 maps, about a year: 1, from 0 to 3.

rows.label: Gerrymandering: discounted years of impact
Gerrymandering: WELLBYs per campaign year, before adjustments
People per year the reforms keep out of prison or jail
rows.explainer: The decarceration branch's people; the phone branches count families' dollars, not people, and are valued per dollar above.

rows.label: Health gained per person affected per year (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Not counted separately: health in prison (and outside it) is part of the life-satisfaction gap above, so counting it again would double it.

rows.label: Income gained per person affected per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: Zero: income is not counted for the people kept out (earnings after release are part of what the life-satisfaction gap measures); the money branches are valued per dollar in fed_uov_per_dollar and st_uov_per_dollar.

rows.label: Probability the win happens because of this work
rows.explainer: Every win counted here is in: the caps are in force and the state laws passed. PPI's part in them is its share of the coalitions' resources (attribution_share below), one question, not two.

rows.label: Years from the win until it takes effect (outcome-weighted average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the two phone branches, for reading only (the WELLBY branches have their own wait rows).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the win takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate (for reading; each branch discounts its own wait).

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
People released, cleared or kept out of detention in the year
rows.explainer: PPI does no casework: nobody is freed by its own lawyers. People kept out by reforms are in the decarceration branch.

rows.label: Years of freedom gained per person released
rows.explainer: No casework (above).

rows.label: Wellbeing gained per year of freedom (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: The same shared gap; it counts nothing here, with no casework.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person released, discounted
Federal caps: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The savings are advocates' and the FCC's projections, not measured bills: 0.85, from 0.6 to 1 (the value of a dollar saved is mechanical).

rows.label: State laws: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The savings are advocates' projections from what families paid before the laws, not measured: 0.85, from 0.6 to 1, as for the federal caps.

rows.label: Federal caps: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: that the caps would have come some day is in the years a win counts (Convention 5, one question each).

rows.label: Federal caps: PPI's share of the campaign's resources
rows.explainer: PPI has campaigned on prison phone rates for two decades (its reports on fees in 2013, video calling in 2015 and the State of Phone Justice in 2019 and 2022, cited in the FCC's proceedings); the Wright petitioners' lawyers, Worth Rises, the United Church of Christ's media justice ministry, Color of Change and others carried the Act and the rulemaking. PPI spends perhaps a fifth of its 1.6 million a year on the issue, about 1.6 million over the five years, against roughly 3 million a year across the coalition over eight years, about 24 million: 7% with its research's weight in the proceedings. The share is PPI's resources in fiscal years 2021-2025 (the cost counted here) over the coalition's over the whole campaign that won the Act and the caps (from about 2017), since PPI's earlier spending isn't in the cost: 7%, from 3% to 18%.

rows.label: Federal caps: share of the savings that holds
rows.explainer: Providers must comply by April 2026; the caps are interim, pending permanent rules, and may change; providers may recover some revenue through charges the caps don't reach; past caps were mostly obeyed: 0.85, from 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: State laws: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: that the laws would have come some day is in the years a win counts (Convention 5).

rows.label: State laws: PPI's share of the campaigns' resources
rows.explainer: Worth Rises led these state campaigns (2020-2023, almost all inside the cost period, so the share is over the whole campaigns) with local coalitions and sponsors; PPI's rate data and testimony supported them: 4%, from 1% to 10%.

rows.label: State laws: share of the savings that holds
rows.explainer: Free calls are paid by the state and run by its contracts; some laws cap free minutes (Connecticut 90 a day): 0.95, from 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: Decarceration: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The wellbeing gap rests on small surveys of prisoners against others not matched to them, and people kept out may face other punishments (probation, fines); the deaths rest on one observational cohort of New York parolees (Patterson 2013), where longer sentences went to people at higher risk anyway (the fact's low end allows for it): 0.75, from 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: Decarceration: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the people count is the reforms' effect, and that they would have come some day is in the years a win counts (Convention 5).

rows.label: Decarceration: PPI's share of the reform movement's resources
rows.explainer: The movement spends hundreds of millions a year (national and state advocacy groups, public defenders' campaigns, foundations); PPI's 1.6 million is under 1% of it, but its data are used widely: 0.5%, from 0.1% to 2%.

rows.label: Decarceration: share of the reforms applied
rows.explainer: 1: the judged count is of people actually kept out, so enforcement is already in it.

rows.label: Federal caps: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the savings are projections and PPI's share is our judgment; no study measures what the caps did to families' bills. The shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: State laws: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the savings are advocates' estimates, two of the five our judgment, and nothing measures PPI's part. The shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Decarceration: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the people kept out are our judgment and the wellbeing gap comes from small surveys. The shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Federal caps: all adjustments combined
State laws: all adjustments combined
Decarceration: all adjustments combined
Gerrymandering: PPI's share of the campaign's resources
rows.explainer: PPI started and led the national campaign (its Prisoners of the Census project) and drafted model bills; state groups and legislators carried them: 50%, from 30% to 80%.

rows.label: Gerrymandering: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the people affected and the value of representation are our judgments. The shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Gerrymandering: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: PPI's share and the missing-data step; the counterfactual is in the years a win counts and the effect is a judgment, so no evidence or enforcement step beyond it.

rows.label: Side effect of decarceration: families and children with a parent home, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Children and partners of people kept out of prison are spared separation and lost income: the shared share (facts/incarceration.json, Wakefield and Wildeman 2013), 15% of the branch's value, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Side effect of decarceration: earnings kept after release, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: A year in prison lowers later earnings, which the life-satisfaction gap of the year inside doesn't cover: the shared share (facts/incarceration.json, Western 2002), 10% of the branch's value, from 0 to 30%.

rows.label: Side effect of decarceration: crime by people not held, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Some people not held commit crimes they would not have committed inside; studies of pretrial reforms mostly find small or no rises in rearrest (Ouss and Stevenson, Does Cash Bail Deter Misconduct?, American Economic Journal: Applied 2023, on Philadelphia's no-bail policy): -10% of the branch's value, from -30% to 0.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: the two phone branches, both in units of value (the decarceration and gerrymandering branches, in WELLBYs and a few percent of the result, have their own rows and are left out so the average needs no exchange rate).

rows.label: Share that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: the two phone branches, both in units of value (the decarceration and gerrymandering branches, in WELLBYs and a few percent of the result, have their own rows and are left out so the average needs no exchange rate).

rows.label: PPI's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: the two phone branches, both in units of value (the decarceration and gerrymandering branches, in WELLBYs and a few percent of the result, have their own rows and are left out so the average needs no exchange rate).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: PPI's share of the resources behind the outcome: the outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (each branch applies its own share).

rows.label: Share of the win that is enforced (outcome-weighted average)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: the two phone branches, both in units of value (the decarceration and gerrymandering branches, in WELLBYs and a few percent of the result, have their own rows and are left out so the average needs no exchange rate).

rows.label: Side effect: more contact with family, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Cheaper calls mean more of them; contact with family in prison is linked to less depression and to fewer returns to prison (studies of visits; a 2026 report linking free calls to better re-entry). Not in the money valued above: 10%, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Side effect: providers cutting service under lower caps, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Providers and jails argued that lower caps would cut phones, hours or security screening; little evidence of it so far: -3%, from -10% to 0.
